explain.say: On 14 July 1789, Parisians stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress-prison, looking for gunpowder. That day is still France's national holiday. Yet within five years the revolution had executed its king and many of its own leaders. Look at the timeline. How did hope turn into terror?

explain.say: Start in 1789. The Estates-General, an old assembly of clergy, nobles and commoners, became a National Assembly. In August it issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man: liberty, equality before the law, power from the nation. See it light up. At this point most people still wanted a king with a constitution. What changed?

explain.say: Watch the chain. In 1791 the king tried to flee and was caught at Varennes, so trust collapsed. In 1792 war with Austria and Prussia brought fear of invasion and traitors. The sans-culottes, working Parisians, pushed the radical Jacobin club, led by figures like Robespierre. Which link made enemies seem to be everywhere?

explain.say: From 1793 the Committee of Public Safety ruled by fear. A Law of Suspects filled prisons. See the sizes, all estimates: about 17,000 people were formally sentenced to death, perhaps 40,000 died in all, and far more died in the civil war in the Vendée in the west. Each number was a person. Why do you think the leaders believed terror was a defence?

draw.text: Figures are estimates; the Vendée total is debated.

explain.say: In July 1794, Thermidor in the revolutionary calendar, Robespierre was overthrown and executed. Now the debate. Marxists like Georges Lefebvre saw a class revolution; revisionists like François Furet saw ideas and political language driving the Terror. Great work. Exam tip: weigh the circumstances of war against the revolution's own ideas.

faq.q: Why did the French Revolution become so violent?
faq.a: The king's flight in 1791, war with Austria and Prussia from 1792, food shortages, civil war and fear of traitors pushed radicals to rule by emergency measures. Historians also point to a political culture that saw opponents as enemies of the people.
asks: What role did the war play?

faq.q: What was the Reign of Terror?
faq.a: The period from about September 1793 to July 1794 when the Committee of Public Safety used arrests, revolutionary courts and the guillotine against suspected enemies. About 17,000 people were formally executed and many more died in prison or civil war.
asks: How many died in the Terror?

faq.q: How do historians interpret the French Revolution?
faq.a: Marxist historians such as Georges Lefebvre and Albert Soboul saw a bourgeois revolution against feudalism. Revisionists such as Alfred Cobban and François Furet challenged this, stressing politics, ideas and language. Many now combine social, cultural and global views.
asks: What is the revisionist view of the French Revolution?

faq.a: Working people of Paris, such as artisans and shopkeepers, named for wearing long trousers instead of the knee-breeches of the rich. They pressed for price controls and radical action.

faq.q: What was the Declaration of the Rights of Man?
faq.a: A statement adopted in August 1789 saying men are born free and equal in rights, that sovereignty lies with the nation and that law must be the same for all. It did not grant women equal rights, which Olympe de Gouges protested in 1791.
asks: What did the Declaration of the Rights of Man say?

facts: The Bastille was stormed on 14 July 1789.
Louis XVI was executed in January 1793.
Robespierre was executed in July 1794, in the month called Thermidor.
